Beállítom Átfogó energiafejlesztési tervet fogadtak el. Bővítik az energiatároló-kapacitásokat, korszerűsítik a villamosenergia-hálózatot, valamint szélenergia- és geotermikus beruházásokat indítanak – mondta Magyar Péter miniszterelnök a kétnapos kormányülés első napja és a védelmi munkacsoport ülése után. A kormányfő a Facebookon közzétett videóban rövid helyzetképet is adott védelmi munkacsoport ülésén elhangzottakról. Az eddigi legforróbb napon vagyunk túl: Budapesten 43 fokot mértek . A Duna vízszintje lassan emelkedik, Paksnál már hét centivel magasabb a vízállás a minimumnál. A kormány kapcsolatban van Szlovákiával; ők nyilvánosan megerősítették, hogy a nemzetközi kötelezettségeiknek eleget tesznek, a Magyarországnak járó vízmennyiséget akadálytalanul továbbengedik. A Dunamenti Erőmű szivattyúja az imént átmeneti időre automatikusan lekapcsolt a hőség miatt, de rövidesen újraindul a termelés. Székesfehérvár mellett egy Mol-telep közelében 150 hektáron égett a száraz avar. A tüzet eloltották. Emellett Dédestapolcsánynál 10 hektáron ég a növényzet, a tüzet jelenleg is honvédségi helikopterekkel oltják. Az ivóvízellátás – nagyon kevés településtől eltekintve – stabil Magyarországon. Ahol segítségre van szükség, ott a katasztrófavédelem és a honvédség jelen van. Sok helyen végeznek vízosztást is köztereken: összesen 140 ezer liter vízzel segítettek a hőségben az elmúlt egy-két napban az autópályákon kialakult torlódásoknál, valamint a vasúton. Magyar megemlítette, hogy a Tisza-frakció 500 önkéntese 35 helyszínen 1 millió liter ivóvizet osztott szét a járókelőknek, az utcákon dolgozóknak és mindazoknak, akiknek a nagy melegben szükségük van rá. A kormány által most bejelentett fejlesztéseket hazai és uniós forrásokból, valamint magántőke bevonásával tervezik megvalósítani. „Olyan konstrukciókat alakítunk ki, amelyek révén a beruházások hasznából a magyar állam és az érintett települések is részesednek” – mondta a kormányfő. Magyar azt mondta, „elődeink számtalan mulasztása és tudatosan rossz döntése vezetett a most kialakult helyzethez. Szándékosan akadályozták a szélerőművek építését Magyarországon, a tárolókapacitások fejlesztése elmaradt. Ha mindezek rendelkezésünkre állnának most, akkor hasonló nehézségekkel bizonyosan nem szembesülnénk.” Az előző kormány az energetikai fejlesztésekre és a klímaváltozáshoz való alkalmazkodásra rendelkezésre álló uniós források hazahozataláról is lemondott – tette hozzá A mostani kormány az uniós források hazahozatalának köszönhetően első lépésben összesen 868 milliárd forintnyi energetikai fejlesztési forrást fog felhasználni – mondta a kormányfő. Augusztus 31-ével kiírják az első szélerőművi pályázatokat a beruházó vállalatoknak. A projektekben magyar állami tulajdonrészt fognak előírni. „Egyértelmű célunk, hogy a beruházásokból a korábbi napelemes fejlesztésekkel szemben a magyar állam és az önkormányzatok anyagilag is részesüljenek” – mondta Magyar Péter. A települések a Szent István Vidékfejlesztési Program keretében pályázhatnak majd a részvételre. Felgyorsítják és átláthatóbbá teszik a háztartási napelemek hálózati csatlakozását. Mindenki számára megnyitják az ingyenes okosmérő-igénylés lehetőségét, és már évi 4000 kWh-s fogyasztás felett kötelezővé teszik a telepítésüket. Egyszerűsítik a geotermikus energia feltárásának engedélyezését. Pénteken eredményt hirdetnek a 1,5 milliárd eurós, azaz közel 600 milliárd forintos elektromoshálózat-fejlesztési, uniós forrásokból megvalósuló pályázaton is. A miniszterelnök külön kiemelte: minél több településnek akarnak lehetőséget nyújtani az energiafejlesztési programban való részvételre. Ez egy település számára sokkal többet jelent néhány szélerőműnél: helyben maradó iparűzési adót, olcsóbb és biztonságosabb energiát, út- és hálózatfejlesztést, valamint hosszú évekre kiszámítható költségvetési bevételt. Olyan forrásokat, amelyekből bölcsődét, rendelőt, utat, közösségi teret vagy éppen vízmegtartó beruházásokat lehet építeni. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: His family said Smyth ‘was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends’, Photograph: Family handout via Salvamont Brașov His family said Smyth ‘was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends’, Photograph: Family handout via Salvamont Brașov Romania Body found in Romania believed to be missing British hiker George Smyth Family paid tribute to Bristol University geology student, 18, after being notified by Avon and Somerset police Nadeem Badshah Sat 15 Aug 2026 13.14 EDT Last modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 13.37 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A body has been found in the search for an 18-year-old British man who went missing last year while hiking in Romania , UK police said. George Smyth, a geology student at the University of Bristol , went missing in November. On Saturday, Avon and Somerset police said a body found in the region of the country is believed to be that of Smyth. His family have been informed and are being supported by a family liaison officer, the force added. Smyth’s family said: “We are all devastated by George’s death. “He was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends. “We want to thank Salvamont mountain rescue, who have worked tirelessly since November searching for George, despite very difficult and often dangerous conditions. “They are an amazing team, and have remained in constant communication, helping us greatly throughout this awful time.” Efforts will be made to return Smyth’s body to the UK once formal identification has taken place. The family’s statement added: “We would also like to thank Avon and Somerset police and University of Bristol, who have gone above and beyond to try and find George, and to support us as a family. “Although this latest news is incredibly painful, the torture of waiting is finally over, so we can now focus on bringing George home and saying goodbye. “We would appreciate privacy while we continue to come to terms with this loss.” On Wednesday, mountain rescue teams said they had resumed their search in “previously indicated areas, under rock walls, in grates and in the hard-to-reach sectors” but without success. The student, from Newport in Shropshire, is believed to have left Poiana Brașov heading to Bran. He reached Țigănești, where he made an emergency call for help. At the time, rescuers said he was in a “very isolated and hard to access mountain area” and the weather conditions were extremely severe with strong winds, heavy snowfall and dense fog. The search and rescue operation also involved a canine unit, drones and helicopters being deployed. Sebastian Marinescu, from the area’s mountain rescue service, previously told the BBC the 18-year-old “was disoriented, physically exhausted, and already showing signs of hypothermia” when they received the emergency call. A munkálatokhoz Magyar Péter szerint „kisebb noszogatásra”, de egészen távoli bányákból is ajánlottak fel követ, mások mellett Orbán Győző, Orbán Viktor apja is . A most részben elkészült dunai fenékküszöb gyors megoldást jelent az atomerőmű működésének biztosítására, ami azóta egyébként újra teljes kapacitással üzemel. Múlt szombaton kezdték el visszakapcsolni a harmadik turbinát, hétfőn négyből három blokk már teljes kapacitáson működött . https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘The EU is slow and cumbersome, built for peacetime. Its membership, while large, is not wide enough, excluding key players in the wider European space.’ Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters View image in fullscreen ‘The EU is slow and cumbersome, built for peacetime. Its membership, while large, is not wide enough, excluding key players in the wider European space.’ Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters Opinion Europe Europe is under attack from three sides – but the EU and Nato are unfit to defend us Nathalie Tocci Ursula von der Leyen’s outreach to Canada and new security proposals are wise – but she may not be the right messenger Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.37 EDT Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.45 EDT Share E urope’s strategic predicament is ever clearer, and ever darker. The continent is at war, which is being fought militarily in Ukraine, but is escalating rapidly across Europe through hybrid attacks. Germany’s disclosure that it blames Russia for the explosion at Leipzig airport; a Russian drone strike on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border; an Italian jet shooting down a Russian drone over Lithuania ; flares fired from a Russian warship at a Danish helicopter – all within the space of a couple of weeks – tell a coherent story. Whether because Russia is bogged down and unable to advance in Ukraine, or because it believes the US will not come to Europe’s rescue, Vladimir Putin’s regime is ever more bent on escalating its aggression in Europe. Canada is seeking new global neighbours – no wonder, as Trump rolls out stupidities at scale | David Moscrop Read more Putin’s calculus is not irrational. Trump never misses a chance to lash out at Europe – the latest example being his threats of further tariffs on the EU if Brussels proceeds to offer Canada “associate membership”. Europeans have grown numb to Trump’s insults and threats, but these threats do underline his deep antipathy, suggesting that if a Russian attack warranted a response, Trump might look the other way. The US certainly can’t be relied on to have Europe’s back. This is the context in which Ursula von der Leyen caused surprise last week by proposing associate membership of the EU for Canada. To bolster Europe’s defences, the European Commission president also wants a “European security council”, and a mutual solidarity mechanism to respond to hybrid attacks. While they have distinct rationales, these ideas fit into the same strategic logic: in a world of predatory powers, the “rest of the west” must huddle together. The threats are not only external. Along with Putin’s Russia and Maga America, the rise of the far right in Europe completes a triangle of threats. The far right is a threat to liberal democracy. But by instigating internal division and pushing for disintegration, it also supports the divide-and-rule designs of predatory external powers, representing a challenge to Europe’s independence and sovereignty. It has taken the earthquake of the AfD’s successes in German regional elections for von der Leyen to acknowledge openly that Europe’s threats are also homegrown. Better late than never. European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato Read more Faced with this unprecedented convergence of threats from three sides, leaders are scrambling for a response. Nato has what it takes to defend Europe against Russia . But if its majority shareholder – the US – is unwilling to step in, the question of its plans, structures and capacities is moot. If a hybrid attack on a European country caused civilian casualties, would Nato be bypassed if Washington signalled its unwillingness to act? Collective defence would not even be invoked if the anticipated result were the US’s betrayal of its European allies. This is where von der Leyen’s emergency protocol comes in, filling the gap between the high-water mark of mutual assistance – article 42.7 of the EU’s founding treaty, which covers armed aggression – and nothing at all. The attacked state would activate the protocol, an emergency European Council would convene, and the commission and EU high representative would propose responses, including evacuation and medical support, stockpiling and energy security, economic coercion, military mobility and more. The mechanism could extend to like-minded non-EU partners, starting with Canada, Norway, the UK and Ukraine. The proposal to offer Canada associate membership, while still undefined, can be read in this light as well. On paper, it all makes sense. In practice, it is hard to see such a mechanism operating seamlessly, let alone rapidly, given the EU’s organisational complexities, its slowness to act and its internal divisions. Hence the proposal for a European security council, consisting of those countries willing and able to contribute to the defence of Europe, without the US if need be. Some of these countries would be EU members, but not all – again, Canada, the UK, Ukraine and possibly Turkey. Both the problem and the solution are clear. To protect itself against predatory powers, what remains of the west must cooperate ever more closely. But the existing multilateral organisations – Nato and the EU – are unfit for purpose. Nato will remain anchored to the US, while the EU is slow and cumbersome, built for peacetime. Its membership, while large, is not wide enough, excluding key players in the wider European space. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Developing alternative forms of EU membership could be of interest not just to Canada, but to the UK, too. The idea was first raised by Berlin for Ukraine, in fact, but Kyiv turned down the offer, seeing it as second-class. Ukraine deserves full EU membership, but if a substantial associate membership is on the table in the short term, it should take that, while continuing to press for more. The rise of far-right nationalism means that reaching consensus within the EU will become harder, not easier – which is precisely where the proposal for a smaller, more agile European security council comes in, provided far-right governments do not simultaneously come to power across major European countries. Von der Leyen’s security proposals are sensible and urgently needed. The potential pitfall lies not in the message, but in the messenger. In her years at the helm of the commission she has grown a reputation for centralising power and overstepping boundaries, irking other EU officials in Brussels as well as European capitals. When it comes to security and defence especially, sovereignty is jealously guarded by the EU’s nation state governments. It would be tragic if European governments ended up killing off a set of good ideas because of Europe’s institutional turf wars. Rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic is the last thing Europe and its partners need right now. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP View image in fullscreen The cost of raising two children has risen to at least $36,500 a year, an increase of 134% in two decades. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP Childcare Australia Cost of raising two children in Australia has risen 134% in two decades, study says Parenting advocate Georgie Dent says rising childcare cost has pushed the overall burden to $36,500 a year and calls for more paid parental leave Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Tom McIlroy Political editor Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.04 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The cost for Australian families of raising two or more children has risen to at least $36,500 a year, according to new research, with the money needed to run a family increasing by 134% in two decades. Data released by advocacy group The Parenthood on Wednesday shows household income has only grown by 102% in the same period, with childcare costs making up 33% of the total cost of having children today. In 2003, the figure was 27%, according to the analysis by firm Connell Griffin. Parenthood chief executive, Georgie Dent, will address the National Press Club in Canberra on Wednesday, arguing that having children reduces the earnings of Australian women by an average of 55% over the first five years of parenthood. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email She will say families need two incomes to stay afloat in the current economy, and even with both parents working, they have less breathing room in their household budget. “For many families it feels like a cruel game of whack-a-mole,” Dent will say. “For parents of young children seeking to raise and provide for their family one obstacle towers over the others: early childhood education and care. “Too many face an impossible bind. They cannot access it, they cannot afford it, or they cannot trust what is available. This isn’t perceived: the options families have are largely determined by what the market has delivered.” Dent will call for a policy pathway from government for the provision of 52 weeks of paid parental leave, up from 26 weeks currently paid for by taxpayers, and meaningful parental leave for fathers and partners. Health, wealth and housing: here’s what forecasters think Australia will look like in 2066 Read more She will push Labor to deliver on its policy aspiration of a universal childcare system, with well paid workers and fee controls and a new national commission established. The speech comes after Monday’s intergenerational report showed that, for the first time, more Australians will be dying than being born in 40 years’ time. Australia’s fertility rate is projected to decline to 1.34 by 2065–66, down from 1.5 children per woman in 2030–31. Fertility rates have been below the replacement rate of 2.1 children per woman for 50 years, contributing to a projected drop in population of 1.7 million people and an increase in the projected median age by 1.7 years in 2065–66. The report found a complex mix of economic, social and cultural factors was to blame, including greater access to contraception, more time spent in education, career development, longer periods living with parents, and delays in forming partnerships and having children. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The treasurer, Jim Chalmers , told Guardian Australia’s weekly Australian Politics podcast on Tuesday that the government remained committed to moving to a universal childcare system in Australia. Pauline Hanson’s stance on paid parental leave and childcare could turn clock back by decades, economists warn Read more Anthony Albanese wants the reform to be part of his political legacy, and the government has commissioned consulting firm Deloitte to help design a universal system. Its report on the policy “pathway” is due in time for the next election. “It is still our ambition,” Chalmers said. “You don’t go from zero to 100. We’ve always seen it as a series of steps.” He pointed to the government’s three-day childcare funding guarantee and the $1bn program to build childcare centres in areas with poor access as significant steps. “It remains the government’s aspiration to get as close to universal as we can,” Chalmers said. https://www.dw.com/en/strong-earthquakes.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O5ce The governor's office in Penonome was severely damaged Image: Martin Bernetti/AFP Advertisement A powerful magnitude-7.7 earthquake struck Panama on Friday morning. According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the quake's epicenter was located approximately 10 kilometers (6 miles) southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, near Panama's southern tip. The quake struck at a depth of 10 kilometers. Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive. The USGS later reported that a second powerful earthquake, measuring 6.6 in magnitude, struck the country following a series of aftershocks. The tremors were strongly felt in the capital Panama City, causing buildings to shake and sending people rushing into the streets. People stand outside a hospital maternity ward in Panama City after the quake Image: Martin Bernetti/AFP "We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we're okay, though we're very scared," Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, where the earthquake struck, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared." Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino described the earthquake as a "major disaster" which had destroyed roads near the epicenter. What do we know about damage? Mulino did not say whether there were any casualties. According to Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service, damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos. Smith reported several injuries, as well as partial collapses and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square, as well as damage to the governor’s office building and the Dos Continentes hotel. Meanwhile, local news outlets reported that the colonial-style Church of San Atanasio in Panama’s Los Santos province collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938. Debris from a damaged building landed on a car Image: Enea Lebrun/REUTERS Tsunami warning lifted The US Tsunami Warning System issued an alert stating that hazardous tsunami waves were possible along parts of the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador, and Mexico within the next three hours. The system also reported a tsunami threat to Hawaii. The warning was lifted later on Friday afternoon. Initially, there were no reports of damage to the Panama Canal. The Panama Canal Authority stated that the waterway was operating as usual. Tocumen International Airport in Panama City briefly suspended operations and activated evacuation protocols before reopening later on Friday afternoon. Panama is located along the so-called "Ring of Fire," a line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes occur. In a particular symbol of stepped up security measures, a helicopter flew over the French capital’s Place de la Republique, one of the epicentres of the unrest, sweeping a powerful searchlight across the square, AFP said. While some restrictions, such as those in Paris, initially applied only for the night from Monday to Tuesday, others, particularly in Bordeaux and Nice, were set to remain in force for several days, the agency noted. Meanwhile, Italy’s government decided to dispatch 500 army troops to Milan after two days of unrest in the city, with shops in the city centre affected by riots and looting.
